title: AI-Generated "Workslop" Is Destroying Productivity
pub: Harvard Business Review (digital article; updated 2025-09-25); research by BetterUp Labs in collaboration with the Stanford Social Media Lab
author: Kate Niederhoffer · Gabriella Rosen Kellerman · Angela Lee · Alex Liebscher · Kristina Rapuano · Jeffrey T. Hancock

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s view that tool access and adoption do not by themselves produce productivity gains, and materially extends it by identifying “workslop”: superficially polished but substantively weak AI output that transfers effort to colleagues. This adds a concrete socio-technical mechanism for weak returns, though it is workplace-wide rather than specific to legal workflows or apprenticeship risks.
qs: In collaboration with Stanford Social Media Lab, our research team at BetterUp Labs has identified one possible reason: Employees are using AI tools to create low-effort, passable looking work that ends up creating more work for their coworkers.

On social media, which is increasingly clogged with low-quality AI-generated posts, this content is often referred to as “AI slop.” In the context of work, we refer to this phenomenon as “workslop.” We define workslop as AI generated work content that masquerades as good work, but lacks the substance to meaningfully advance a given task.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s distinction between AI adoption and realised organisational value, and materially extends it by identifying “workslop” as a mechanism through which superficially polished but weak output shifts verification and rework onto colleagues. Its survey-based cost estimates also add evidence about productivity and interpersonal harms, though it does not propose a redesign or governance response.
qs: In collaboration with Stanford Social Media Lab, our research team at BetterUp Labs has identified one possible reason: Employees are using AI tools to create low-effort, passable looking work that ends up creating more work for their coworkers.
Based on participants’ estimates of time spent, as well as on their self-reported salary, we find that these workslop incidents carry an invisible tax of $186 per month.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that productivity depends on task suitability, human guidance and workflow practices rather than access or usage alone. It also reinforces the cluster’s warning that indiscriminate adoption can impose downstream rework and collaboration costs; its adoption-frequency findings do not establish productivity gains.
qs: Gen AI is not appropriate for all tasks, nor can it read minds.
Gen AI gives us a new technology with which to lean into the same old bad habits—but now with the added cost of creating more work for our colleagues and undermining collaboration, at scale.

kp.k: Growing AI adoption does not necessarily deliver measurable returns
kp.d: The article, updated September 25, 2025, frames a cross-industry productivity puzzle: companies with fully AI-led processes nearly doubled in the preceding year and workplace AI use doubled since 2023, yet a report attributed to the MIT Media Lab found no measurable investment return at 95% of organizations. The authors propose workslop as one possible explanation, not as an established explanation for the entire reported return gap.
qs: Consider, for instance, that the number of companies with fully AI-led processes nearly doubled last year, while AI use has likewise doubled at work since 2023.
Yet a recent report from the MIT Media Lab found that 95% of organizations see no measurable return on their investment in these technologies.

In collaboration with Stanford Social Media Lab, our research team at BetterUp Labs has identified one possible reason: Employees are using AI tools to create low-effort, passable looking work that ends up creating more work for their coworkers.

kp.k: Workslop transfers cognitive effort rather than eliminating it
kp.d: The authors define workslop as superficially credible AI-generated content that fails to advance a task. They distinguish polishing substantive work from producing incomplete, unhelpful or context-deficient slides, reports, summaries and code. Their central mechanism is downstream burden shifting: recipients must interpret, correct or redo output, so apparent ease for the creator creates additional human work elsewhere.
qs: We define workslop as AI generated work content that masquerades as good work, but lacks the substance to meaningfully advance a given task.
The insidious effect of workslop is that it shifts the burden of the work downstream, requiring the receiver to interpret, correct, or redo the work.
Unlike this mental outsourcing to a machine, however, workslop uniquely uses machines to offload cognitive work to another human being.

kp.k: Survey reports widespread workslop across organizational hierarchies
kp.d: In an ongoing survey of 1,150 U.S.-based full-time employees across industries, 40% reported receiving workslop in the last month. Those encountering it estimated that 15.4% of received workplace content qualified. The article reports peer-to-peer transmission at 40%, direct reports sending it to managers at 18%, and downward transmission at 16%. Professional services and technology were disproportionately affected; these are cross-industry findings rather than a separately reported legal-sector study.
qs: Of 1,150 U.S.-based full-time employees across industries, 40% report having received workslop in the last month.
Employees who have encountered workslop estimate that an average of 15.4% of the content they receive at work qualifies.
The phenomenon occurs mostly between peers (40%), but workslop is also sent to managers by direct reports (18%).
Sixteen percent of the time workslop flows down the ladder, from managers to their teams, or even from higher up than that.
Workslop occurs across industries, but we found that professional services and technology are disproportionately impacted.

kp.k: Recipient accounts describe checking, coordination and rework burdens
kp.d: Quoted survey participants illustrate the proposed mechanism rather than establish its frequency. A finance individual contributor described choosing between rewriting, returning work or accepting it; a technology frontline manager described spending an hour or two assembling colleagues to clarify an email; a retail director described independent research, supervisory meetings and redoing the work.
qs: It created a situation where I had to decide whether I would rewrite it myself, make him rewrite it, or just call it good enough.
It probably took an hour or two of time just to congregate [sic] everybody and repeat the information in a clear and concise way.

I had to waste more time following up on the information and checking it with my own research. I then had to waste even more time setting up meetings with other supervisors to address the issue. Then I continued to waste my own time having to redo the work myself.

kp.k: Estimated productivity costs depend on self-reported time and salaries
kp.d: Employees reported an average of one hour and 56 minutes spent on each instance. Using estimated time and self-reported salaries, the authors calculate a $186 monthly workslop tax and extrapolate over $9 million annually for an organization of 10,000 workers. That extrapolation uses 41% prevalence, whereas the earlier survey summary reports 40%; the article presents these as estimates rather than directly measured organization-wide losses.
qs: Employees reported spending an average of one hour and 56 minutes dealing with each instance of workslop.
Based on participants’ estimates of time spent, as well as on their self-reported salary, we find that these workslop incidents carry an invisible tax of $186 per month.
For an organization of 10,000 workers, given the estimated prevalence of workslop (41%), this yields over $9 million per year in lost productivity.

kp.k: Workslop damages perceived competence, trust and willingness to collaborate
kp.d: Respondents reported annoyance (53%), confusion (38%) and offense (22%). Approximately half viewed senders as less creative, capable and reliable; 42% viewed them as less trustworthy and 37% as less intelligent. Some 34% notified teammates or managers, and 32% reported reduced willingness to work with the sender again. The authors warn that these interpersonal effects threaten collaboration and AI adoption over time, distinguishing that prospective concern from respondents' reported reactions.
qs: When we asked participants in our study how it feels to receive workslop, 53% report being annoyed, 38% confused, and 22% offended.
Approximately half of the people we surveyed viewed colleagues who sent workslop as less creative, capable, and reliable than they did before receiving the output.
Forty-two percent saw them as less trustworthy, and 37% saw that colleague as less intelligent.
What’s more, 34% of people who receive workslop are notifying teammates or managers of these incidents, potentially eroding trust between sender and receiver.
One third of people (32%) who have received workslop report being less likely to want to work with the sender again in the future.

kp.k: Separate research suggests an AI-use competence penalty
kp.d: The authors compare their interpersonal findings with separate research in which engineers allegedly using AI to write code were perceived as less competent than engineers who did not, with female engineers disproportionately penalized. They present the connection as a possible echo of that research, not as a finding that their own workslop survey establishes a gender-specific effect.
qs: This may well echo recent research on the competence penalty for AI use at work, where engineers who allegedly used AI to write a code snippet were perceived as less competent than those who didn’t (and female engineers were disproportionately penalized).

kp.k: Indiscriminate AI mandates encourage indiscriminate use
kp.d: The authors argue that ubiquitous-use mandates model poor task selection and passing responsibility onward. They recommend organizational policies covering best practices, tools and norms while preserving employee autonomy. AI can improve some work, but complex or ambiguous tasks still require thoughtful human guidance and feedback; these are management recommendations grounded in the authors' research and implementation experience.
qs: When organizational leaders advocate for AI everywhere all the time, they model a lack of discernment in how to apply the technology.
Gen AI is not appropriate for all tasks, nor can it read minds.
To be sure, AI can positively transform some aspects of work, but it still requires thoughtful guidance and feedback from workers in order to produce useful outputs on complex or ambiguous work.
While employees should be invested with autonomy around AI, the organization should be working through its own careful policies and recommendations around best practices, top tools, and norms.

kp.k: Agency and optimism distinguish purposeful from avoidance-oriented AI use
kp.d: Drawing on workforce adoption research tracked since 2023, the authors label high-agency, high-optimism workers 'pilots' and low-agency, low-optimism workers 'passengers.' Pilots use generative AI 75% more often at work and 95% more often outside work. The authors also report that pilots are more likely to enhance creativity, whereas passengers are more likely to avoid work. These are reported associations between mindset and usage, not evidence that increasing adoption alone reduces workslop.
qs: Our labs have been tracking predictors of gen AI adoption across the workforce since 2023 and we found that workers with a combination of high agency and high optimism are much more likely to adopt gen AI than those with low agency and low optimism.
Pilots use gen AI 75% more often at work than passengers, and 95% more often outside of work.
Pilots are much more likely to use AI to enhance their own creativity, for example, than passengers.
Passengers, in turn, are much more likely to use AI in order to avoid doing work than pilots.

kp.k: AI integration requires collaborative accountability and unchanged quality standards
kp.d: The authors frame prompting, feedback and context provision as collaborative activities whose consequences extend to colleagues. They recommend integrating AI products into shared workflows for shared outcomes, setting acceptable-use guardrails, modeling purposeful use and retaining the same standards for human-AI work as for human-only work. Their broader argument is that AI scales familiar shortcut-taking habits unless organizations prioritize responsibility and useful outcomes over activity.
qs: So many of the tasks required to work well with AI—giving prompts, offering feedback, describing context—are collaborative.

Seamless collaboration in 2025 must include the ways we incorporate AI work products into our common workflows, in service of shared outcomes, rather than as a vehicle for subversively dodging responsibility.
Set clear guardrails for your teams around norms and acceptable use.
Frame AI as a collaborative tool, not a shortcut.
And uphold the same standards of excellence for work done by bionic human-AI duos as by humans alone.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors claim that low-substance AI-generated work shifts effort from its creator to coworkers, imposing productivity costs and damaging collaboration; purposeful, guided use can instead enhance work.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain workplace source, not a study of legal services. Niederhoffer and coauthors define 'workslop' as polished AI-generated content that does not meaningfully advance a task. They argue that recipients must decode, check, correct or redo it, so apparent individual efficiency creates downstream work. They present this as one possible explanation for disappointing organizational AI returns, not the sole explanation. Reported consequences include time costs, annoyance, diminished assessments of senders' capability and trustworthiness, and reduced willingness to collaborate. The authors predict that these interpersonal effects can undermine collaboration and AI adoption over time. They also argue that blanket AI-use mandates encourage undiscriminating use, whereas purposeful use, human guidance, clear norms and unchanged quality standards can support useful outcomes. Their 'pilots' and 'passengers' are employee mindset categories: high-agency, optimistic workers reportedly use AI more often and more purposefully, while low-agency, low-optimism workers are more likely to use it to avoid work.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The primary evidence is an ongoing survey of 1,150 U.S. full-time employees, supplemented by respondent accounts, prior adoption research, external reports and the authors' organizational experience.
pts.d: The authors report that 40% of respondents received workslop in the preceding month; those encountering it estimated that it constituted 15.4% of received work content. Respondents reported an average of one hour and 56 minutes spent per incident. The authors derive a $186 monthly cost from self-reported time and salary and extrapolate more than $9 million annually for a 10,000-worker organization using 41% prevalence, rather than the earlier rounded 40%. These are survey-based cost estimates and a hypothetical organizational extrapolation, not directly measured company losses. Emotional responses included annoyance (53%), confusion (38%) and offense (22%). Approximately half viewed senders as less creative, capable and reliable; 42% viewed them as less trustworthy and 37% as less intelligent. Thirty-four percent notified colleagues or managers, and 32% reported less willingness to work with the sender again. Anonymous finance, technology and retail respondents describe rewriting, clarification meetings and independent checking. Separate lab research tracking adoption since 2023 associates high agency and optimism with more frequent AI use: 'pilots' reportedly use it 75% more often at work and 95% more often outside work than 'passengers.' For context, the article cites an MIT Media Lab report's claim that 95% of organizations see no measurable AI investment return and external research on perceived competence penalties for AI use, including a disproportionate penalty for female engineers. These external findings are not presented as results of the workslop survey. Recommendations draw on research and experience assisting Fortune 500 companies; the document does not report a controlled test of the recommended interventions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article describes current workplace experiences in 2025, using a preceding-month survey window, and forecasts cumulative collaboration risks without specifying a deadline.
pts.d: The supplied article was updated September 25, 2025. The workslop survey is described as recent and ongoing; the text does not provide exact fieldwork dates. Receipt prevalence concerns the last month, while costs are expressed per incident, monthly and through an annual extrapolation. The separate adoption research has run since 2023. Longer-term damage to collaboration is framed as a threat 'over time,' not as an established longitudinal finding or dated forecast. The central harm claim concerns unhelpful, incomplete or context-poor AI output, not all AI-assisted work: the authors explicitly distinguish polishing good work from producing workslop. They qualify potential benefits by task suitability and the need for thoughtful human guidance and feedback on complex or ambiguous tasks. Their recommendations assume deliberate leadership, employee responsibility and integration into shared workflows.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Recipients bear rework costs, senders face reputational and collaboration penalties, and organizations face productivity losses; professional services and technology are reported as disproportionately affected.
pts.d: The survey covers U.S.-based full-time employees across industries. The authors report workslop moving between peers (40%), from direct reports to managers (18%), and downward from managers or higher leadership (16%); the text does not enumerate all remaining flows. Recipients must interpret, research, clarify and redo content, sometimes while navigating sensitive hierarchical relationships. Senders risk being perceived as less capable or trustworthy and becoming less desirable collaborators. Employers bear the estimated productivity costs and potential erosion of collaboration. Leaders are assigned responsibility for discerning AI-use policies, tool guidance and quality norms. Professional services and technology are singled out as disproportionately impacted, but no legal-industry subgroup results, law-firm effects or client outcomes are provided. Finance, technology and retail respondent accounts illustrate individual experiences rather than sector-wide estimates.
